screens.title: Introduction to Amazon EC2
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build an intuitive model of Amazon EC2 and why it matters for developers. EC2 provides resizable virtual servers you can rent from the cloud, giving you full control over the operating system, network, and software stack. We'll connect that idea to AMIs, which are templates that carry an image of an operating system and applications, and instance types, which decide the virtual hardware your instance gets. You'll see how key pairs enable secure SSH or RDP access and how security groups operate as instance-level firewalls. Practical relevance is constant: when you choose an instance type you balance performance and cost, when you pick an AMI you standardize deployments, and when you design security group rules you reduce attack surface. A concrete example you'll see later is launching a t2. micro Amazon Linux 2 instance, creating a key pair, opening HTTP for your web site, and allowing SSH only from a trusted IP. A common misconception is thinking cloud servers are managed for you; in fact you manage OS updates, keys, and firewall rules. Keep that in mind as we explore each component and the hands-on workflow you'll follow.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will be able to explain EC2 instance concepts, AMIs, and key pairs: that means defining a virtual server, describing how AMIs carry OS and apps, and explaining why instance types matter. Second, you will launch and configure a basic EC2 instance using both the console and the CLI; this includes choosing an AMI, picking an instance type, associating a key pair, and applying a security group. Third, you will implement and manage security groups to control network access; you will design rules to allow required protocols while restricting administrative ports. Fourth, you will identify common misconfigurations and follow best practices, such as restricting SSH to known IPs and safeguarding private keys. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can demonstrate mastery during labs and quizzes. These skills are central for developers who deploy applications to AWS, because they combine system knowledge, secure access, and repeatable launch workflows.

screens.title: What is an EC2 instance?
screens.narratorSegment: An EC2 instance is a virtual server that you can provision and manage in AWS. Think of it like renting a physical machine in a data center, except the cloud gives you elasticity: you can choose compute size, start or stop instances, and scale horizontally. The instance itself is a running copy of an AMI on an instance type. A concrete example is launching an Amazon Linux 2 image on a t2. micro instance to host a small web server. Practically, when you launch an instance you decide the operating system and software via the AMI, and the hardware profile via the instance type; you also attach a security group and a key pair for access. A misconception is assuming AWS manages your application-level updates: while AWS runs the underlying virtualization, you remain responsible for OS patches, application deployments, and key management. To check understanding, ask: if you need more memory for a database workload, which part do you change—the AMI or the instance type? The correct answer is the instance type. Key takeaway: EC2 gives flexible, user-managed virtual machines that you can tune for workload needs.

keyIdea.title: EC2 = User-managed virtual machine
keyIdea.text: You provision and control the OS and software; AWS provides the underlying compute infrastructure.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is an EC2 instance?
A rentable virtual server you control, suitable for web servers, databases, and development tasks.
  • EC2 instances are virtual machines launched from an AMI and assigned an instance type for CPU/memory.
  • Instances provide full OS-level control: you install, patch, and configure software yourself.
  • They can be started, stopped, resized, and replaced to meet changing demand.
Example
Launch Amazon Linux 2 on t2.micro to host a low-traffic web site during development.
Common mistake
Assuming AWS will update your OS and apps automatically; you must manage patches yourself.
Key Takeaway

An EC2 instance is your virtual server: choose AMI for software and instance type for hardware, and manage updates yourself.

Annotated concept cards
AMI
Software image used to boot the instance.
Instance Type
Defines CPU, memory, and network capacity.
Security
You attach key pairs and security groups to control access and traffic.
Try this reflection: if your app needs more memory, change the instance type rather than the AMI.

screens.title: Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)
screens.narratorSegment: An Amazon Machine Image, or AMI, is a template that contains the operating system, any installed applications, and configuration settings needed to launch an EC2 instance. AMIs let you reproduce the same software environment across multiple instances, which is essential for consistent deployments. For example, you can create a custom AMI from a fully configured instance with your web server and application pre-installed, then use that AMI to launch identical instances across environments. A common misunderstanding is thinking AMIs define hardware; they do not. AMIs capture software state while instance types determine C P U, memory, storage, and network capabilities. From a practical perspective, use official AMIs for base operating systems, marketplace AMIs for specialized stacks, and custom AMIs when you need standardization and fast scaling. When building automation, referencing an AMI ID ensures every launched instance has the same baseline. Key takeaway: treat AMIs as build artifacts for your instances—version them, secure credentials before creating them, and choose the right source image for your workload. Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) means use amis to capture and reproduce a software environment; they do not set hardware characteristics.. In practical terms, templates that package an operating system and application software. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
What an AMI contains
An operating system, libraries, application server, and optionally applications and configuration.
AMIs let you launch instances that start from a known software state.
Create custom AMIs from configured instances to standardize deployments.
Use official or marketplace AMIs as a secure base when possible.
Example
Build an AMI from an instance with Nginx and your app pre-installed to speed scaling.
AMI best practices
  • Secure secrets before baking an AMI—do not include private keys or credentials.
  • Version your AMIs so you can roll back to known-good images.
  • Prefer minimal base images and install only what you need for predictability.
Pro Tip

Use automated pipelines to bake AMIs so images are reproducible and tested before use in production.

screens.title: Instance Types: choosing compute profiles
screens.narratorSegment: Instance types define the virtual hardware profile for an EC2 instance: C P U, memory, storage performance, and network capability. AWS groups instance types by optimization goals: general purpose families such as t-series and m-series are balanced for a wide range of workloads, compute optimized c-series prioritize C P U, memory optimized r-series prioritize R A M, and storage optimized i-series and d-series are tuned for high input and output. When you choose an instance type you are trading cost against capability. For example, a t2. micro is suitable for low-traffic development servers, while compute-heavy batch jobs need a c-series instance for faster processing. A common mistake is selecting an oversized instance for cost reasons without measuring workload behavior; start with monitoring and scale to a larger type if C P U or memory saturates. Another misconception is conflating AMIs with instance types—they serve different roles: AMIs define software, instance types define hardware. Key takeaway: pick the instance type that matches your workload profile, monitor performance, and adjust to balance cost and throughput. Instance Types: choosing compute profiles means choose a family optimized for your workload: general-purpose, compute, memory, or storage optimized.. In practical terms, how cpu, memory, storage, and network shape performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture
Instance Type Families
Families are grouped by optimization goal—balance, compute, memory, or storage.
General purpose (t, m)
Balanced CPU and memory for common workloads.
Compute optimized (c)
Higher CPU for compute-bound applications.
Memory optimized (r)
Higher RAM for in-memory databases and caches.
Storage optimized (i, d)
Designed for heavy I/O workloads and local storage performance.
Choosing an instance type
  • Start with a general purpose instance for unknown workloads and monitor.
  • If CPU is consistently high, consider compute optimized; if memory is constrained, choose memory optimized.
  • For disk-heavy workloads prefer storage optimized families.
Key Takeaway

Match the instance family to workload needs, monitor utilization, and change instance type to optimize cost and performance.

screens.title: Key Pairs and Secure Access
screens.narratorSegment: Key pairs are the authentication mechanism for accessing EC2 instances without passwords. AWS stores the public key and you keep the private key file—typically a. pem file for Linux or. ppk for Windows. When you connect, the server uses the public key to verify a challenge from the client that proves possession of the private key. A concrete scenario: you create a key pair named my-web-server-key, download the. pem file, set strict file permissions, and use it to authenticate via SSH. Two important practical points: never share or check private keys into source control, and if you lose the private key there is no recovery path for that key pair on the instance—you must create a new instance or replace authorized keys through another access method. A common misconception is believing keys are stored server-side for retrieval; only the public key is stored by AWS. Key takeaway: safeguard private keys, restrict SSH to trusted IPs, and treat private keys as sensitive credentials. Key Pairs and Secure Access means aws stores the public key; you store the private key and use it to authenticate to your instances.. In practical terms, how public and private keys protect ssh and rdp connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Key pair = secure credential pair
keyIdea.text: AWS stores the public key; you store the private key and use it to authenticate to your instances.

content.html:
Core Concept
Key Pairs
A public-private key pair grants SSH or RDP access without passwords.
Public key is stored by AWS and placed on the instance.
Private key is downloaded once and must be stored securely by you.
If the private key is lost, you cannot use it to access the instance again.
Example
Create a key pair, download my-web-server-key.pem, set permissions, and use it to SSH into the instance.
Common mistake
Checking private keys into code repositories or emailing them around.
Practical guidance
  • Download the private key once and restrict file permissions (read-only for owner).
  • Rotate keys by creating new key pairs and updating instance authorized keys when needed.
  • Use IAM and session managers when you need auditable access without long-lived private keys.
Key Takeaway

Protect private keys like passwords. Losing a private key means losing direct access to instances tied to it.

screens.title: Security Groups: instance-level firewalls
screens.narratorSegment: Security groups act as virtual firewalls attached to EC2 instances. They are stateful rule sets that specify allowed inbound protocols, ports, and source ranges, and allowed outbound traffic. For example, a web-server security group commonly allows inbound HTTP on port 80 and HTTPS on port 443 from anywhere, while restricting SSH on port 22 to a specific office IP range. Security groups are applied to instances at launch or attached later, and they can be reused by multiple instances. A common misconception is that security groups function like host-based firewalls inside the instance; while they control network traffic at the instance level in AWS, you still often use OS-level firewalls inside the instance for defense-in-depth. Practical guidance: use the principle of least privilege—allow only required ports and limit source CIDR ranges for administrative access. If you open SSH to all IPs, you are exposing your instance to attackers; always prefer precise ranges. Key takeaway: security groups are your first line of network defense for EC2 instances and should be as restrictive as your access model allows. Security Groups: instance-level firewalls means define least-privilege rules for inbound and outbound traffic; prefer narrow source ranges for admin ports.. In practical terms, control inbound and outbound traffic with fine-grained rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Security Group Workflow
Create, define rules, attach to instances, and test access.
Step 1: Create SG
Name and initial description.
Step 2: Add rules
Allow HTTP/HTTPS for web, SSH only from trusted IPs.
Step 3: Attach to instance
Apply during launch or associate later.
Example: web-server-sg
Inbound rules: HTTP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0, HTTPS 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, SSH 22 from your office CIDR only.
Common mistake
Leaving SSH open to all IPs or using overly permissive outbound rules.
Key Takeaway

Security groups control traffic to instances. Restrict admin access and keep service ports minimal.

screens.title: Launch a basic EC2 instance (Console)
screens.narratorSegment: Launching an EC2 instance from the AWS Management Console is a guided process that helps you make repeatable choices. Start at the EC2 dashboard and choose Launch instance; then pick an AMI such as Amazon Linux 2 or Ubuntu Server, and select an instance type like t2. micro for low-traffic workloads. Create or choose a key pair and download the private key—store it securely. Configure a security group that allows HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443) from anywhere for the web server, while limiting SSH (port 22) to your IP range. Finally, review and launch. A practical example: when you launch a t2. micro with Amazon Linux 2, note the instance's public IPv4 address to connect. Common misconceptions include skipping the security group review and leaving SSH open to all; always verify your firewall rules before launching. This console flow is valuable for beginners and for quick manual testing, while automation with the CLI or SDK is better for repeatable deployments. After launch, you will connect to the instance and install a web server in a later lesson. Launch a basic EC2 instance (Console) means select ami, choose instance type, create/download key pair, configure security group, review, and launch.. In practical terms, step-by-step guided workflow to start an amazon linux 2 t2.micro. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Select AMI, choose instance type, create/download key pair, configure security group, review, and launch.

content.html:
Process Flow
Launch steps (Console)

CLI example (visual)
Below is a representative CLI snippet you will use in automation. Use region-specific AMI and security group identifiers when you run this in your environment.

screens.title: Connect via SSH and install Nginx
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting to your Linux EC2 instance requires the private key and the instance's public IP address. Before connecting, set file permissions on the private key to be read-only for the owner. Use the standard SSH username for the AMI—ec2-user for Amazon Linux or ubuntu for Ubuntu images—and authenticate with the private key. Once connected, update packages and install a web server such as Nginx; then start and enable the service so it persists across reboots. For example, on Amazon Linux you update packages and install Nginx using the distribution's package manager, then start the service and enable it at boot. A common mistake is forgetting to set private key permissions, which causes SSH clients to reject the key. Another is forgetting to open HTTP in the security group, which leaves the server unreachable from a browser. Key takeaway: secure your private key, confirm network rules, and verify the web server by opening the instance's public IP in a browser to see the default Nginx page. Live Lab
SSH and web server commands (visual)
Visual examples of the sequence you'll run in the terminal. Keep these commands in the terminal panel while you follow along.
chmod 400 my-web-server-key.pem

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: When working with EC2, several recurrent mistakes can lead to security incidents or operational friction. One common misconfiguration is leaving SSH open to all IP addresses; this invites automated attacks and increases risk. A second is mishandling private keys—sharing them or checking them into repositories—because anyone with the private key can access your instance. A third is conflating AMIs and instance types: selecting the wrong instance type can waste cost or degrade performance, while baking secrets into an AMI can leak credentials across all instances started from it. Best practices to prevent these problems include restricting SSH to known IP ranges, protecting private keys and rotating them if compromised, and using the principle of least privilege for security groups. Also, automate AMI creation and instance launches in CI/CD so images and parameters are versioned and repeatable. A useful verification step is to inspect security group rules and ask whether each open port is strictly necessary. Takeaway: simple checks during launch and disciplined handling of keys and images greatly reduce risk. Common mistakes and best practices means restrict ssh, protect private keys, avoid embedding secrets in amis, and follow least-privilege rules for security groups.. content.html:
Comparison
Common Misconfigurations
Open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0
Allows broad access and increases attack surface.
Private keys exposed
Leaked keys permit unauthorized access.
Secrets baked into AMIs
Every instance launched from the AMI inherits the secret.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build an intuitive model of Amazon EC2 and why it matters for developers. EC2 provides resizable virtual servers you can rent from the cloud, giving you full control over the operating system, network, and software stack. We'll connect that idea to AMIs, which are templates that carry an image of an operating system and applications, and instance types, which decide the virtual hardware your instance gets. You'll see how key pairs enable secure SSH or RDP access and how security groups operate as instance-level firewalls. Practical relevance is constant: when you choose an instance type you balance performance and cost, when you pick an AMI you standardize deployments, and when you design security group rules you reduce attack surface. A concrete example you'll see later is launching a t2. micro Amazon Linux 2 instance, creating a key pair, opening HTTP for your web site, and allowing SSH only from a trusted IP. A common misconception is thinking cloud servers are managed for you; in fact you manage OS updates, keys, and firewall rules. Keep that in mind as we explore each component and the hands-on workflow you'll follow.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will be able to explain EC2 instance concepts, AMIs, and key pairs: that means defining a virtual server, describing how AMIs carry OS and apps, and explaining why instance types matter. Second, you will launch and configure a basic EC2 instance using both the console and the CLI; this includes choosing an AMI, picking an instance type, associating a key pair, and applying a security group. Third, you will implement and manage security groups to control network access; you will design rules to allow required protocols while restricting administrative ports. Fourth, you will identify common misconfigurations and follow best practices, such as restricting SSH to known IPs and safeguarding private keys. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can demonstrate mastery during labs and quizzes. These skills are central for developers who deploy applications to AWS, because they combine system knowledge, secure access, and repeatable launch workflows.

These objectives translate directly into demonstrable actions in the lab. For explanation, you will map terminology to architecture: define an EC2 instance, an AMI, instance types, key pairs, and security groups. For launching, you will complete a guided process to start a t2. micro instance and verify it's reachable. For security groups, you will author rules that permit web traffic and limit SSH to a known IP range. For misconfigurations, you will inspect an instance and point out overly permissive rules or misplaced private keys. Each card corresponds to a verified competency milestone: an assessment will ask you to configure a security group, to launch an instance from a chosen AMI, and to demonstrate secure SSH access. Practically, these tasks prepare you to automate deployments in CI/CD pipelines and reduce human error when provisioning servers. Remember, the goal is not only to run an instance but to do it repeatedly, securely, and with minimal privileges.

An EC2 instance is a virtual server that you can provision and manage in AWS. Think of it like renting a physical machine in a data center, except the cloud gives you elasticity: you can choose compute size, start or stop instances, and scale horizontally. The instance itself is a running copy of an AMI on an instance type. A concrete example is launching an Amazon Linux 2 image on a t2. micro instance to host a small web server. Practically, when you launch an instance you decide the operating system and software via the AMI, and the hardware profile via the instance type; you also attach a security group and a key pair for access. A misconception is assuming AWS manages your application-level updates: while AWS runs the underlying virtualization, you remain responsible for OS patches, application deployments, and key management. To check understanding, ask: if you need more memory for a database workload, which part do you change—the AMI or the instance type? The correct answer is the instance type. Key takeaway: EC2 gives flexible, user-managed virtual machines that you can tune for workload needs.

An Amazon Machine Image, or AMI, is a template that contains the operating system, any installed applications, and configuration settings needed to launch an EC2 instance. AMIs let you reproduce the same software environment across multiple instances, which is essential for consistent deployments. For example, you can create a custom AMI from a fully configured instance with your web server and application pre-installed, then use that AMI to launch identical instances across environments. A common misunderstanding is thinking AMIs define hardware; they do not. AMIs capture software state while instance types determine C P U, memory, storage, and network capabilities. From a practical perspective, use official AMIs for base operating systems, marketplace AMIs for specialized stacks, and custom AMIs when you need standardization and fast scaling. When building automation, referencing an AMI ID ensures every launched instance has the same baseline. Key takeaway: treat AMIs as build artifacts for your instances—version them, secure credentials before creating them, and choose the right source image for your workload. Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) means use amis to capture and reproduce a software environment; they do not set hardware characteristics.. In practical terms, templates that package an operating system and application software. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Instance types define the virtual hardware profile for an EC2 instance: C P U, memory, storage performance, and network capability. AWS groups instance types by optimization goals: general purpose families such as t-series and m-series are balanced for a wide range of workloads, compute optimized c-series prioritize C P U, memory optimized r-series prioritize R A M, and storage optimized i-series and d-series are tuned for high input and output. When you choose an instance type you are trading cost against capability. For example, a t2. micro is suitable for low-traffic development servers, while compute-heavy batch jobs need a c-series instance for faster processing. A common mistake is selecting an oversized instance for cost reasons without measuring workload behavior; start with monitoring and scale to a larger type if C P U or memory saturates. Another misconception is conflating AMIs with instance types—they serve different roles: AMIs define software, instance types define hardware. Key takeaway: pick the instance type that matches your workload profile, monitor performance, and adjust to balance cost and throughput. Instance Types: choosing compute profiles means choose a family optimized for your workload: general-purpose, compute, memory, or storage optimized.. In practical terms, how cpu, memory, storage, and network shape performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Key pairs are the authentication mechanism for accessing EC2 instances without passwords. AWS stores the public key and you keep the private key file—typically a. pem file for Linux or. ppk for Windows. When you connect, the server uses the public key to verify a challenge from the client that proves possession of the private key. A concrete scenario: you create a key pair named my-web-server-key, download the. pem file, set strict file permissions, and use it to authenticate via SSH. Two important practical points: never share or check private keys into source control, and if you lose the private key there is no recovery path for that key pair on the instance—you must create a new instance or replace authorized keys through another access method. A common misconception is believing keys are stored server-side for retrieval; only the public key is stored by AWS. Key takeaway: safeguard private keys, restrict SSH to trusted IPs, and treat private keys as sensitive credentials. Key Pairs and Secure Access means aws stores the public key; you store the private key and use it to authenticate to your instances.. In practical terms, how public and private keys protect ssh and rdp connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Security groups act as virtual firewalls attached to EC2 instances. They are stateful rule sets that specify allowed inbound protocols, ports, and source ranges, and allowed outbound traffic. For example, a web-server security group commonly allows inbound HTTP on port 80 and HTTPS on port 443 from anywhere, while restricting SSH on port 22 to a specific office IP range. Security groups are applied to instances at launch or attached later, and they can be reused by multiple instances. A common misconception is that security groups function like host-based firewalls inside the instance; while they control network traffic at the instance level in AWS, you still often use OS-level firewalls inside the instance for defense-in-depth. Practical guidance: use the principle of least privilege—allow only required ports and limit source CIDR ranges for administrative access. If you open SSH to all IPs, you are exposing your instance to attackers; always prefer precise ranges. Key takeaway: security groups are your first line of network defense for EC2 instances and should be as restrictive as your access model allows. Security Groups: instance-level firewalls means define least-privilege rules for inbound and outbound traffic; prefer narrow source ranges for admin ports.. In practical terms, control inbound and outbound traffic with fine-grained rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Launching an EC2 instance from the AWS Management Console is a guided process that helps you make repeatable choices. Start at the EC2 dashboard and choose Launch instance; then pick an AMI such as Amazon Linux 2 or Ubuntu Server, and select an instance type like t2. micro for low-traffic workloads. Create or choose a key pair and download the private key—store it securely. Configure a security group that allows HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443) from anywhere for the web server, while limiting SSH (port 22) to your IP range. Finally, review and launch. When working with EC2, several recurrent mistakes can lead to security incidents or operational friction. One common misconfiguration is leaving SSH open to all IP addresses; this invites automated attacks and increases risk. A second is mishandling private keys—sharing them or checking them into repositories—because anyone with the private key can access your instance. A third is conflating AMIs and instance types: selecting the wrong instance type can waste cost or degrade performance, while baking secrets into an AMI can leak credentials across all instances started from it. Best practices to prevent these problems include restricting SSH to known IP ranges, protecting private keys and rotating them if compromised, and using the principle of least privilege for security groups. Also, automate AMI creation and instance launches in CI/CD so images and parameters are versioned and repeatable. A useful verification step is to inspect security group rules and ask whether each open port is strictly necessary. Takeaway: simple checks during launch and disciplined handling of keys and images greatly reduce risk. Let's summarize the essential concepts to remember. Amazon EC2 is the service that provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud as virtual servers. An Amazon Machine Image, or AMI, is the software template that contains the operating system and applications used to launch an instance. Instance types define the virtual hardware profile—C P U, memory, storage, and network capabilities—so choose a family that matches your workload. These three building blocks—EC2, AMI, and instance type—compose the foundation of any server deployment on AWS. Finish with the security essentials. A key pair is a public-private key credential pair where AWS stores the public key and you retain the private key to authenticate to instances. Security groups are virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic for EC2 instances; apply least-privilege rules and restrict administrative ports to trusted IP addresses. Finally, the principle of least privilege appears throughout: open only necessary ports, avoid embedding secrets in AMIs, and automate deployments so images and configurations are versioned. These security rules are not optional: they protect access, limit attack surface, and make your deployments safer and easier to manage.
